title: Chances for the next word
objectives: Turn a row of next-word counts into probabilities that add up to 1.

screens.title: How likely is cat?
screens.prose: The row for “the” in our next-word table: cat 3, mat 1, jam 1, dog 1. Pick one of the pairs that start with “the” at random, each pair equally likely.

state.caption: The row for “the”: six pairs start with “the”.

screens.question: What is the chance that the word after “the” is “cat”? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: How many pairs start with “the”?
Add the four bars: that is the row total.
3 of the 6 pairs go on to cat: $\tfrac36 = \tfrac12$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac12$: three of the six pairs go on to cat.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide cat's count by the number of pairs that start with “the”.

byKey.words: You divided by the 20 words of the text. Divide by the 6 pairs that start with “the”.
byKey.count: 3 is the count. A chance divides it by the row total.
byKey.different: You divided by the 4 different words. Divide by the 6 pairs instead.

explain.text: Six pairs start with “the”, and three of them go on to cat. Each pair is one equally likely draw, so the chance is $\tfrac36 = \tfrac12$.

screens.title: Count over row total
screens.prose: You divided a count by the **row total**: the number of pairs that start with the word now. With each pair equally likely, that is the chance of the next word, as in counting: what we want over everything.

state.caption: The row for “the”: six pairs start with “the”.

screens.question: Fill in the chance of each word after “the”, as a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: The row total is 6.
cat $\tfrac36 = \tfrac12$; mat, jam and dog $\tfrac16$ each.

feedback.correct: cat $\tfrac12$, and $\tfrac16$ each for mat, jam and dog.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide each count by the row total, 6.

byKey.words: $\tfrac1{20}$ divides by the 20 words. Only the 6 pairs that start with “the” count.

explain.text: Each count over the row total of 6: cat $\tfrac36 = \tfrac12$, the others $\tfrac16$ each. They add to $\tfrac36 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac16 + \tfrac16 = 1$, and every row's chances do.

screens.title: The row for cat
screens.prose: The row for “cat” is sat 1, ate 1, “.” 1.
screens.question: What is the chance that “ate” comes after “cat”? Give a fraction.

hints.text: How many pairs start with “cat”?
Three bars of 1.
1 of 3: $\tfrac13$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide ate's count by the row total.

byKey.count: 1 is the count. Three pairs start with “cat”, so divide by 3.
byKey.words: You divided by the 20 words. Divide by the 3 pairs that start with “cat”.

explain.text: Three pairs start with “cat”, one for each word, so each chance is $\tfrac13$. A tie in the counts is a tie in the chances.

screens.title: The row for sat
screens.prose: “sat” appears twice in the text, and “on” follows it both times.
screens.question: What is the chance that “on” comes after “sat”?

hints.text: How many pairs start with “sat”, and how many of them end in “on”?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide on's count by the row total.

byKey.count: 2 is the count. Divide by the 2 pairs that start with “sat”.
byKey.words: You divided by the 20 words. The row total is 2.

explain.text: Both pairs that start with “sat” end in “on”, so the chance is $\tfrac22 = 1$. A chance of 1 means certain: this table always writes “on” after “sat”.

screens.title: A text of your own
screens.prose: A new text of 16 words about a fund.
screens.question: What is the chance that “rose” comes straight after “fund”? Give a fraction.

hints.text: Find each “fund” and the word after it.
“fund” appears three times.
rose twice, fell once: $\tfrac23$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac23$: rose twice and fell once after “fund”.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the pairs that start with “fund”.

byKey.words: You divided by the 16 words. Only the 3 pairs that start with “fund” count.
byKey.different: You split the chance evenly between rose and fell. Count the pairs: rose 2, fell 1.

explain.text: “fund” starts three pairs: rose twice and fell once. So rose has chance $\tfrac23$ and fell $\tfrac13$, adding to 1.

screens.title: Which total?
screens.prose: A classmate wants the chance that “dog” comes after “the”. She divides its count, 1, by the 20 words of the text.

state.caption: The row for “the”: six pairs start with “the”.

screens.question: What is the right chance? Give a fraction.

hints.text: Which pairs could end in “dog” after “the”?
Only these six pairs start with “the”.
1 of 6: $\tfrac16$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the row total.

byKey.words: That is her mistake: 20 counts every word in the text. Only the 6 pairs that start with “the” can end in “dog”.
byKey.different: You divided by the 4 different words after “the”. They are not equally likely: cat has 3 of the 6 pairs.
byKey.pairs: You divided by all 19 pairs. Only the 6 that start with “the” count.

explain.text: A chance divides by the row total, the pairs that start with the word now. Here that is 6, so dog has $\tfrac16$. Dividing by 20 gives chances in the row that add to only $\tfrac{6}{20}$.

screens.title: Seen once
screens.prose: “dog” appears once in the text, followed by “sat”. So the table gives “sat” a chance of 1 after “dog”.
screens.question: How far should we trust that chance of 1?

options.text: Not far: it rests on one example
Fully: a chance of 1 means certain
options.why: Here 1 is one example out of one. One more sentence such as “the dog ran” would change it.

options.text: Not at all: counted chances are wrong
options.why: Counting is the method; it needs many examples to be reliable.

hints.text: How many times did the table see “dog”?
Once, so every chance in its row is 0 or 1.

feedback.correct: Not far: one example makes the table sure.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about how much text the row rests on.

byKey.fully: The table is certain only because it saw “dog” once.

explain.text: With one example, every chance in the row is 0 or 1, so the table is sure of something it saw once. A longer text with “the dog ran” would split the row. This is one reason real models learn from huge amounts of text.

screens.title: Chances in code
screens.prose: A row is a list of counts, such as `[3, 1, 1, 1]` for “the”.
screens.question: Write `chances(counts)`: return each count divided by the row total, in the same order.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each list is compared number by number with math.isclose.

mutants.symptom: Divides by the number of different next words instead of the row total.
Divides by the 20 words of the course text instead of the row total.
Adds one too many to the total, so the chances add to less than 1.

hints.text: Add up the counts first, in a loop.
Then append `c / total` for each count `c`.

feedback.correct: Your function divides each count by the row total.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: `[3, 1, 1, 1]` has row total 6: the answer starts with 0.5.
byKey.test-3: One count of 2 is a row with one word: its chance is 1.

explain.text:
Add the counts once to get the row total, then divide each count by it. The results add to 1, because the counts add to the total.

```python
total = 0
for c in counts:
    total = total + c
```

screens.title: Chances from a row
screens.prose: For a word $a$ that starts at least one pair: $$\text{chance of } b \text{ after } a = \frac{\text{count of } a \to b}{\text{row total for } a}$$ The chances in a row add up to 1.
screens.question: A row has counts 4, 3 and 1. What is the chance of the first word? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Find the row total first.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide 4 by the row total.

byKey.count: 4 is the count. Divide it by the row total, 8.
byKey.even: You shared the chance evenly between three words. The counts differ, so divide each by 8.

explain.text: The row total is $4 + 3 + 1 = 8$, so the first word has $\tfrac48 = \tfrac12$. The other two have $\tfrac38$ and $\tfrac18$, and the three add to 1.

screens.title: Up after up
screens.prose: A share's daily moves over a year make a next-move table with two words, up and down. After an up day came 68 up days and 62 down days. After a down day came 61 up and 58 down.
screens.question: What is the chance the share rises tomorrow, given it rose today? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: Which row is “today up”, and what is its total?
The row for an up day.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide 68 by the total of the up row.

byKey.column: You divided by the 129 days that were up next. Divide by the 130 pairs that start on an up day: the row total.
byKey.all: You divided by all 249 pairs. Only the 130 that start on an up day count.

explain.text: The row for up holds $68 + 62 = 130$ pairs, so the chance is $\tfrac{68}{130} \approx 0.523$. That is close to a half, so this table says little about tomorrow.

ideas: A next word's chance is its count over the row total: the number of pairs that start with the word now.
The chances in a row add up to 1.
A row seen only a few times gives chances of 0 or 1 that rest on too little text.

formula.name: Chance of the next word
formula.tex: \text{chance of } b \text{ after } a = \dfrac{\text{count of } a \to b}{\text{row total for } a}
formula.note: Divide by the row total, not by the words in the text.

summary.trap: Dividing by the 20 words of the text, or by the 4 different next words, instead of the row total of 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide by the row total, 4.

byKey.count: 2 is the count. Divide it by the row total, 4.

explain.text: The row total is 4, so the first word has $\tfrac24 = \tfrac12$.

quiz.question: What is the chance of the second word? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide 3 by the row total.
